cards.front:
**Choose an identity management solution — Determine if an OIDC server is needed**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

Web apps require a way to *remember* past actions because the web, by default, is stateless. Otherwise, users would be forced to enter their credentials every time they navigated to a new page. The common solution for remembering state is *cookies*, a browser-based mechanism for storing data. The web server sends the initial cookie, then the browser stores it and sends it back with each request. This is done automatically without the need for the developer to write any code. Cookies are easy to use and built into the browser but are designed for use within a single website or web domain. The default solution that is built into ASP.NET Core uses cookie-based authentication.

Tokens are containers with metadata that are explicitly passed through the headers or body of HTTP requests. The main advantage of tokens over cookies is that they are not tied to a specific app or domain. Instead, tokens are usually *signed* with asymmetric cryptography. For example, OIDC servers issue tokens with information about identity using the [JSON Web Token (JWT)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSON_Web_Token) format which includes signing. Asymmetric cryptography uses a combination of a private key known only to the signer, and a public key which everyone can know. Tokens may also be encrypted. 

The signed token can't be tampered with due to the private key. The public key:

* Makes it possible to validate the token to ensure it hasn't been changed.
* Guarantees that it was generated by the entity holding the private key.

The main disadvantage to using tokens is that they require a service (typically an OIDC server) to both issue and provide validation for tokens. The service must be installed, configured, and maintained.

A common reason an OIDC server is required is for applications that expose web-based APIs that are consumed by other apps. For exposed web-based APIs, client UIs such as Single Page Applications (SPA), mobile clients, and desktop clients are considered to be part of the same app. SPA examples include Angular, React, and Blazor WebAssembly. If apps other than your web app or any client UIs must make a secure API call to your app, you'll likely want to use tokens. If you only have client UIs, ASP.NET Core Identity provides the option to acquire a token during authentication. The authentication token issued by ASP.NET Core Identity:

* Can be used by mobile and desktop clients. Cookies are preferred over tokens for both security and simplicity.
* Isn't suitable for managing access from third-party apps.

Another reason an OIDC server is required is for sharing sign-ins with other apps. Commonly referred to as *single sign on*, this feature enables users to:

* Sign in once with a web app's form.
* Use the resulting credentials to authenticate with other apps without having to sign-in again or choose a different password.

An OIDC server is typically preferred to provide a secure and scalable solution for single sign on. 

For apps that don't share logins with other apps, the simplest way to quickly secure an app is to use the built-in ASP.NET Core Identity provider. Otherwise, an OIDC server provided by a third-party identity management solution is needed. OIDC servers are available as:

* Products you install on your server, called *self-host*.
* Containers run in a host like Docker.
* Web-based services you integrate with to manage identity.

Some solutions are free and open source, while others are commercially licensed. See identity management solutions for a list of available options. It's possible that your organization already uses an identity provider. In that case, it may make sense to use the existing provider instead of going with a different solution. All of the major solutions provide documentation for configuring ASP.NET Core to use their product or service.

**ASP.NET Core security topics — Authentication vs. Authorization**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

Authentication is a process where a user provides credentials that are compared to credentials stored in an operating system, database, app, or resource. When the two sets of credentials match, the user authenticates successfully. They can then perform actions for which they're authorized. The authorization process determines the actions the user is allowed to do.

Another way to think of authentication is to consider it as a way to **enter** a space, where the space is a server, database, app, or resource. Authorization defines **what actions** the user can perform to which objects inside that space (server, database, or app).

## Key idea

A web app that redirects to a URL that's specified via the request such as the query string or form data can potentially be tampered with to redirect users to an external, malicious URL. This tampering is called an open redirection attack.

Whenever your application logic redirects to a specified URL, you must verify that the redirection URL hasn't been tampered with. ASP.NET Core has built-in functionality to help protect apps from open redirect (also known as open redirection) attacks.

**Work with SameSite cookies in ASP.NET Core — History and changes**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

SameSite support was first implemented in ASP.NET Core in 2.0 using the [2016 draft standard](https://tools.ietf.org/html/draft-west-first-party-cookies-07#section-4.1). The 2016 standard was opt-in. ASP.NET Core opted-in by setting several cookies to `Lax` by default. After encountering several [issues](https://github.com/aspnet/Announcements/issues/318) with authentication, most SameSite usage was [disabled](https://github.com/aspnet/Announcements/issues/348).

[Patches](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/net-core-November-2019/) were issued in November 2019 to update from the 2016 standard to the 2019 standard. The [2019 draft of the SameSite specification](https://github.com/aspnet/Announcements/issues/390):

* Is **not** backwards compatible with the 2016 draft. For more information, see [Supporting older browsers](https://github.com/dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs/blob/c8ab8d7254e1b3cafa82eee538939c82d88cc8e5/aspnetcore/security/samesite.md#sob) in this document.
* Specifies cookies are treated as `SameSite=Lax` by default.
* Specifies cookies that explicitly assert `SameSite=None` in order to enable cross-site delivery should be marked as `Secure`. `None` is a new entry to opt out.
* Is supported by patches issued for ASP.NET Core 2.1, 2.2, and 3.0. ASP.NET Core 3.1 or later has additional SameSite support.
* Is scheduled to be enabled by [Chrome](https://chromestatus.com/feature/5088147346030592) by default in [Feb 2020](https://blog.chromium.org/2019/10/developers-get-ready-for-new.html). Browsers started moving to this standard in 2019.

**ASP.NET Core 2.1 Razor Pages SameSite cookie sample — Setting Cookie Authentication and Session State cookies**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

Cookie authentication, session state and [various other components](https://github.com/dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs/blob/c8ab8d7254e1b3cafa82eee538939c82d88cc8e5/aspnetcore/security/samesite.md)
set their sameSite options via Cookie options, for example

```csharp
services.AddAuthentication(CookieAuthenticationDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddCookie(options =>
    {
        options.Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.None;
        options.Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always;
        options.Cookie.IsEssential = true;
    });

services.AddSession(options =>
{
    options.Cookie.SameSite = SameSiteMode.None;
    options.Cookie.SecurePolicy = CookieSecurePolicy.Always;
    options.Cookie.IsEssential = true;
});
```

In the preceding code, both cookie authentication and session state set their sameSite attribute to `None`, emitting the attribute with a `None` value, and also set the Secure attribute to `true`.

cards.front:
Why must authentication always happen before authorization in a backend system?

**A.** Both processes run simultaneously, so order does not matter at all.

**B.** Authentication requires permission checks before identity can be confirmed.

**C.** You cannot decide what permissions to grant until you know who the user is.

**D.** Authorization verifies identity, so it cannot work without authentication first.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**C.** You cannot decide what permissions to grant until you know who the user is.

## Lesson context

Imagine walking into a high-security office building. At the front desk, the security guard asks for your ID card to prove who you are. Once the guard verifies that your face matches the card, you walk through the lobby. However, when you try to swipe that same card to enter the executive server room, the scanner flashes red and denies you entry.

This everyday scenario perfectly illustrates the two pillars of web security: **Authentication** and **Authorization**. While they sound similar and work together closely, they handle completely different jobs in a backend system.

Authentication decides who you are. It's the process of verifying a user's identity. It answers one fundamental question, *"Is this person who they claim to be?"*

When a user registers for an account, they provide a unique identifier, such as a username, email, a password, and other credentials. This information is then stored securely in the database. The next time the user visits and tries to log in, the backend system compares the credentials they type against the records stored in the database.

Backend developers use three main categories of factors to authenticate users:

- **Something you know:** A password, a PIN, or the answer to a security question.

- **Something you have:** A physical smartphone receiving an SMS verification code, or a temporary token from an authenticator app.

- **Something you are:** Biometric data like a fingerprint or a facial recognition scan.

Once the system successfully authenticates the user, **Authorization** takes over and decides what the user is allowed to do or access. It answers a different question, *"What permissions does this specific identity have?"*

Just because a user successfully logs in does not mean they should have total control over the application. Authorization defines the rules, roles, and boundaries for that user. Consider these common application roles:

- **Standard User:** Can edit their own profile, but they cannot view other users' private billing information.

- **Editor:** Can write and publish blog posts, but they cannot delete the entire website codebase.

- **Admin:** Has full clearance to modify databases, delete users, and change system-wide settings.

In backend code, authorization usually happens via middleware functions that check a user role or specific permissions before granting access to certain pages or data.

To get these straight, remember this simple rule: **Authentication must always happen first, then authorization.** You cannot decide what permissions to give someone until you know exactly who they are.

Authentication is the key that opens the front door, and authorization decides which rooms you can enter once you are inside.

---

What is the core vulnerability that enables a CSRF attack?

**A.** The server stores passwords in plain text instead of hashed format.

**B.** The browser automatically attaches cookies to any request going to the target server.

**C.** The user refuses to log out of websites after completing their session.

**D.** The backend encrypts all session data with a weak algorithm.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**B.** The browser automatically attaches cookies to any request going to the target server.

## Lesson context

In the last two lectures, you learned how to verify the user identity and maintain their session using cookies. However, automatically sending cookies with every request introduces a unique security vulnerability called Cross-Site Request Forgery, CSRF.

CSRF is an attack that forces an authenticated user to execute unwanted actions on a web application where they are currently logged in. In a CSRF attack, a malicious website tricks the victim browser into making a fraudulent request to your backend server, exploiting the server trust in the user browser cookie.

To understand CSRF, consider this step-by-step example of a banking application:

1. **The Setup:** You log into your bank website, say, `trusted-bank.com`. The bank validates your credentials and stores a session token in your browser cookie.

2. **The Trap:** Without logging out of your bank, you open a new browser tab and visit a malicious website, say `evil-hacker-site.com`.

3. **The Trigger:** The malicious website contains a hidden script or a form that automatically submits a request to the bank backend, such as `POST trusted-bank.com/transfer?amount=1000&to=hacker`.

4. **The Execution:** Because you are still logged into your bank, your browser automatically appends your bank session cookie to that request. The bank server sees a valid cookie, assumes you made the request intentionally, and transfers your money.

The critical takeaway here is that the malicious website cannot read your cookie or steal your data directly. Instead, it simply piggybacks on the fact that your browser automatically attaches cookies to any request going to the target server.

There are two primary defenses: the **SameSite Cookie Attribute** and **CSRF Tokens**.

The simplest defense is setting the `SameSite` attribute on your cookies. This tells the browser when it is allowed to send the cookie along with cross-site requests.

- **SameSite=Strict:** The browser never sends the cookie if the request originates from a third-party website.

- **SameSite=Lax:** The browser allows cookies only when a user safely navigates to the target site, such as clicking a standard link, but blocks them on cross-site form submissions or API requests.

For robust protection, backend frameworks use CSRF tokens. When a user loads a page, the backend generates a random, unique, and unpredictable token and attaches it to the frontend form or session.

When the client submits a request, they must include this token in the custom request headers or form data. The backend compares the submitted token against the token saved in the user session. Because a malicious website cannot access your frontend to copy this secret token, any cross-site request they forge will lack this token and fail validation.

By implementing these strategies, you ensure that requests arriving at your backend are intentional actions made by the actual user, rather than unauthorized actions forced by a malicious player.

What are the three distinct parts that make up a JSON Web Token (JWT) string?

**A.** Algorithm, data, and secret key.

**B.** Header, body, and footer.

**C.** Metadata, claims, and hash.

**D.** Header, payload, and signature.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**D.** Header, payload, and signature.

## Lesson context

In the previous lecture, you learned how a backend server identifies a user during login. But what happens after they log in? How does the server remember who they are when they navigate to a new page? This is where JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) come in.

In plain English, a JWT is a digital keycard that the server issues to a user after a successful login. The user presents this keycard to the server on every subsequent request to prove their identity without re-entering their password.

Instead of the server remembering every active user in its own memory, it shifts the responsibility to the client using a simple four-step process:

1. **Login:** The user sends their username and password, or other means of login, to the server.

2. **Issue:** The server verifies the credentials against the credentials that were stored when they signed up. If they are correct, the server generates a JWT and sends it back to the user.

3. **Storage:** The client receives the JWT and stores it, typically in a browser cookie or local storage.

4. **Request:** For every future request to a protected route, the client automatically sends the JWT along. The server verifies the token and grants access.

A JWT looks like a long, chaotic string of characters. It consists of three distinct parts separated by two dots, like this:

```bash
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3OCIsIm5hbWUiOiJKYW5lIERvZSIsImFkbWluIjp0cnVlLCJpYXQiOjE1MTYyMzkwMjJ9.Lfu39gE9OI8rhPXbmJMorXTtVappkNMw9xq-M4HXttA
```

The first part is the **Header**, the second is the **Payload**, and the third part is the **Signature**.

The **header** is an encoded JSON object that tells the server what type of token it is (JWT) and which hashing algorithm was used to secure it, such as HMAC SHA256.

The **payload** is the middle part of the token. It contains the actual data, or "claims" about the user. This is where you store information like the user ID, username, or account role such as admin or user.

One important security note is that the header and payload are only encoded (Base64), not encrypted. This means anyone can easily decode them and read the data inside. So, never store sensitive data like raw passwords or credit card numbers inside a JWT payload.

The **signature** is the final and most crucial part of the token. The server takes the encoded header, the encoded payload, and mixes them together with a secret key known only to the server. It then hashes them to create the signature.

The signature prevents tampering. If a user tries to decode their token, change their role from "user" to "admin", and re-encode it, the signature will no longer match the altered data.

When the server receives the modified token, it attempts to recreate the signature using its secret key. Because the payload changed, the calculated signature will not match the token's signature, and the server will instantly reject the request with a 401 Unauthorized status code.

In short, JWTs allow stateless authentication. The server does not need to store session data in a database, it simply trusts the token because the signature proves the server itself created it.

cards.front:
What is the primary purpose of the Content-Security-Policy header set by Helmet?

**A.** To hide the server technology from automated scanners.

**B.** To prevent Cross-Site Scripting by restricting allowed script sources.

**C.** To disable clickjacking attacks on the website.

**D.** To force browsers to communicate exclusively over HTTPS.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**B.** To prevent Cross-Site Scripting by restricting allowed script sources.

## Lesson context

When building web applications, your backend server does more than just send data, it also sends hidden information back to the browser in the form of HTTP response headers.

By default, Express configurations expose details about your server technology. Attackers can exploit these default headers to find vulnerabilities in your app. This is why developers use Helmet.js.

Helmet.js is a security middleware collection for Node.js applications. It acts as a protective shield by automatically setting, modifying, or removing specific HTTP headers.

By managing these headers, Helmet helps protect your application from common web vulnerabilities, malicious scripts, and data sniffing attacks.

Instead of requiring you to configure dozens of security protocols manually, Helmet configures a suite of smaller middleware functions out of the box. Installing it takes a single terminal command:

```bash
npm install helmet
```

To apply this security blanket to your entire Express application, you require only one line of code:

```js
const express = require('express');
const helmet = require('helmet');

const app = express();

// apply Helmet security middleware
app.use(helmet());
```

By placing `app.use(helmet())` at the top of your middleware stack, Helmet intercepts every outgoing response and configures your HTTP headers securely.

When you initialize Helmet, it handles several critical security jobs automatically. Here are the most important configurations it sets:

**Hiding server technology (X-Powered-By)**: By default, Express advertises itself by sending the header `X-Powered-By: Express`. This tells hackers exactly what technology your backend runs on, allowing them to target version-specific bugs. Helmet completely removes this header, forcing attackers to guess your underlying setup blindly.

**Mitigating cross-site scripting (Content-Security-Policy)**: Content Security Policy (CSP) is one of the most powerful defenses against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. Helmet establishes strict rules defining where the browser is allowed to load scripts, images, and styles from. This prevents malicious injectors from running unauthorized scripts in your users' browsers.

**Preventing clickjacking (X-Frame-Options)**: Clickjacking occurs when a malicious site embeds your website inside an invisible iframe, tricking users into clicking buttons they did not intend to click. Helmet sets the `X-Frame-Options` header to `SAMEORIGIN`, ensuring your website cannot be embedded on external, untrusted domains.

**Enforcing secure connections (Strict-Transport-Security)**: Helmet forces browsers to communicate with your server exclusively over secure HTTPS connections rather than insecure HTTP. This protects data from being intercepted by attackers on the same network.

In short, Helmet provides a vital layer of defense for production applications. While it does not fix bugs in your custom code, it instantly hardens your server configuration against automated scanners and common exploitation techniques.

cards.front:
How does the smartphone manufacturer example demonstrate security without privacy?

**A.** The data is encrypted but shared with law enforcement.

**B.** The data is safely stored but sold to advertisers without permission.

**C.** The data is public but protected from hackers by a strong firewall.

**D.** The data is deleted regularly but backed up on external drives.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**B.** The data is safely stored but sold to advertisers without permission.

## Lesson context

**Security protects data from unauthorized access, theft, and malicious damage.** It builds a strong digital wall around your information online.

Think of data security as a heavy lock on your front door. The lock keeps intruders out of your house. In the digital world, security focuses on safeguarding data confidentiality, data integrity, and system availability.

Cybersecurity tools include network firewalls, strong passwords, data encryption, and antivirus software. If an outside hacker tries to steal your files, security systems block the attempt.

Security does not analyze what the data means. It only focuses on keeping the data safe from bad actors. Without security, any data you store online remains vulnerable to immediate theft.

**Privacy controls how organizations collect, store, use, and share your personal data.** It gives you the power to dictate who sees your private information.

Look at data privacy as a window curtain. Even if your window has a strong lock, people can see inside if you leave the curtain wide open.

Privacy ensures that companies respect your personal rights. It dictates whether a company can sell your browsing history, track your GPS location, or share your email address with third-party advertisers.

Global laws like the GDPR from the European Union (EU) strictly regulate data privacy. You will learn about those laws in a coming lecture.

Now let's look at the relationship between security and privacy. Though they are distinct concepts, they closely depend on each other.

You can easily have security without having privacy. For instance, a smartphone manufacturer might store your daily location data in a highly secure cloud database. Advanced hackers cannot breach this server, so the data remains entirely safe from bad actors online.

However, if the manufacturer sells that data to advertising agencies without your explicit permission, then your privacy is compromised. The security works perfectly, but your data privacy is zero.

On the other hand, you can never achieve true privacy without robust security. If a medical clinic promises never to share your health records, they are promising privacy. But if the clinic fails to secure their local servers, a rogue hacker can easily steal those medical records.

This complete lack of security instantly destroys your data privacy. Therefore, robust security acts as the essential foundation for effective privacy.

Security provides the technical defense mechanism, while privacy governs the legal rights and policies concerning data usage. Understanding this difference helps you navigate the digital space safely.

Security teams build technical defenses against active cyberattacks, while privacy teams ensure compliance with privacy laws and respect user choices.

Both elements remain essential to protect individuals online today. Security locks the front door, and privacy draws the window blinds. Together, they create a safe, trustworthy environment for your personal information.

cards.front:
What three specific parts make up a web origin under the Same-Origin Policy?

**A.** The browser version, the operating system, and the device type.

**B.** The user agent, the IP address, and the session token.

**C.** The HTML version, the CSS framework, and the JavaScript engine.

**D.** The web protocol, the domain name, and the port number.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**D.** The web protocol, the domain name, and the port number.

## Lesson context

The Same-Origin Policy is a built-in safety measure in your web browsers that stops one website from reading private data from another website. This rule protects your personal accounts from hackers.

An origin has three specific parts: the web protocol, the domain name, and the port number.

For example, in the address `https://example.com:443`, the protocol is HTTPS, the domain name is `example.com`, and the port number is `443`.

Browsers often hide the port number if it is the standard one. HTTPS defaults to port 443, and HTTP defaults to port 80. Even if hidden, the browser still checks it. Two websites have the same origin only when all three of these parts match exactly.

Under this strict rule, a browser blocks a website from prying on a different website. Imagine you open your online bank account in one browser tab and you open a malicious website in a second tab. The same-origin policy blocks the malicious website from stealing your banking info.

However, modern websites often need to share data across different origins. For example, a frontend webpage might need to pull data from a separate backend server. The same-origin rules in browsers block these safe requests, so developers needed a way to share data securely. This is where CORS comes in.

CORS is a system that lets servers open access through browser rules. It uses special headers to grant data access to trusted sites.

Here's what happens when your browser asks another site for data:

* It includes an `Origin` header which names the website making the request
* The receiving server then checks this name
* If the server trusts the website, it replies with a special permission header which tells the browser that the website is allowed to read the incoming data.

If the server does not send this permission, the browser blocks the data instantly. The frontend website then gets an error message instead of the private files.

In Node.js applications using Express, CORS is implemented with the `cors` package:

```javascript
const express = require('express');
const cors = require('cors');
const app = express();

// this enables CORS for all origins and all routes for development
app.use(cors());
```

In production, you might have to pass a configuration object to restrict access to a specific domain:

```javascript
const corsOptions = {
  origin: ['https://yourapp.com', 'https://admin.yourapp.com'],
  credentials: true
};

app.use(cors(corsOptions));
```

If you're using raw Node.js, you would have to handle it manually by setting the CORS response headers yourself on every request:

```javascript
res.setHeader('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', 'https://example.com');
res.setHeader('Access-Control-Allow-Methods', 'GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS');
res.setHeader('Access-Control-Allow-Headers', 'Content-Type, Authorization');
```

cards.front:
What cryptographic protocol does HTTPS use to secure the transfer of data between a browser and a web server?

**A.** Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) only.

**B.** Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP).

**C.** Transport Layer Security (TLS).

**D.** File Transfer Protocol (FTP).
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**C.** Transport Layer Security (TLS).

## Lesson context

HTTPS stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure. It is the secure version of HTTP.

As you've learned in a few previous lectures, HTTP transfers data between your browser and a website. Standard HTTP sends this data in plain text, so anyone can intercept that plain text data.

For this reason, HTTPS uses a cryptographic protocol called Transport Layer Security (TLS) to secure this data transfer. TLS encrypts the communication channel between two points. Older systems used Secure Sockets Layer (SSL), which many web hosting platforms still use today.

Encryption scrambles that data into unreadable code that only the user's browser and the web server hold the keys to unscramble.

For example, when you type a password into a website, HTTPS scrambles it instantly and protects credit card information, personal addresses, login credentials, and other sensitive information. Hackers who intercept the data see only random characters, so they cannot use the stolen information.

This protection is vital on public Wi-Fi networks. Open Wi-Fi networks at coffee shops, airports, and other public places lack basic security, giving cybercriminals the ability to monitor unencrypted traffic on these networks. HTTPS creates a private tunnel through the public network to keep your browsing history safe from nearby bad actors.

HTTPS also provides authentication, which proves that a website is legitimate. To use HTTPS, a website owner must obtain a digital certificate that a trusted organization issues. The certificate verifies the true identity of the website owner.

When you visit a website and the address starts with only "http", that's one way to know that the website owner has not obtained that certificate, making the website unsafe. Modern browsers also warn you about such websites.

Lastly, data integrity is another key benefit of HTTPS. This means no one can alter your data during transit. A hacker cannot inject malicious code into the website files while they travel to your device. You receive the exact data that the website owner sent.

Search engines like Google prioritize HTTPS websites, as safe websites rank higher in search results. Modern browsers also require HTTPS for advanced features such as geolocation, push notifications, and web cameras.

cards.front:
What often happens when companies rush to launch new products and treat security as an afterthought?

**A.** They skip thorough code reviews and deep security testing.

**B.** They hire additional security staff to compensate for speed.

**C.** They delay the launch to conduct more security training.

**D.** They release stable software with minimal coding errors.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**A.** They skip thorough code reviews and deep security testing.

## Lesson context

When it comes to security, the first line of action and prevention is the companies and teams that deploy software, because security issues rarely happen by chance. Security issues occur when these companies rush their processes, ignore fundamental software design principles, or fail to train their staff adequately.

A major trigger for security issues is **the rapid pressure to deliver results**. When a company rushes to launch a new product, development teams often treat security as an afterthought. They skip thorough code reviews and rush past deep security testing to meet strict deadlines.

This speed creates unstable software full of coding oversights, missing access controls, and unpatched bugs that hackers can easily exploit.

Another frequent situation involves **complex system integration**. Modern applications rely heavily on external libraries, third-party APIs and microservices.

When developers bring these different technologies together, they introduce a massive supply chain of risks.

If an open-source tool contains a vulnerability, or if an external vendor suffers a data breach, that security failure automatically spreads into the main application.

**Poor configuration management** also causes massive security issues. This situation happens when tech teams deploy servers or cloud databases using standard factory settings.

Default configurations frequently include blank administrator passwords, open network ports, and public data access privileges. Attackers use automated internet scanners to hunt for these unconfigured systems and gain instant access.

**Human error during daily operations** is another high-risk situation. Employees face constant social engineering attacks such as phishing emails, fraudulent text messages, and deceptive phone calls.

If workers do not receive proper security awareness training, they can be tricked into revealing their personal login credentials, clicking malicious download links, or transferring company data to fraudulent accounts.

Lastly, **security issues occur during organizational mergers and corporate restructuring**. When two unique companies combine their digital networks, IT staff must connect completely different software setups quickly.

This transition often creates blind spots that could lead to the security team losing visibility over old servers, misconfiguring network firewalls, or granting excessive access permissions to users who do not need them.

cards.front:
What is the main difference between first-party and third-party cookies?

**A.** First-party cookies are stored in the browser, while third-party cookies are stored on the server.

**B.** First-party cookies track your actions on the website you visit, while third-party cookies track you across different websites.

**C.** First-party cookies require user permission, while third-party cookies do not require any consent.

**D.** First-party cookies are always secure, while third-party cookies are always insecure.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**B.** First-party cookies track your actions on the website you visit, while third-party cookies track you across different websites.

## Lesson context

Cookies are small text files that websites save on your device to remember some information about you.

Here's the process of receiving and storing cookies:

- You visit a website
- The website server sends a `Set-Cookie` header in its response
- Your browser receives the header and saves the cookie file on your computer hard drive
- Every other time you visit that website, your browser automatically sends the cookie back to the server

This process lets the website remember your login session, shopping cart items, preferences and settings, and other critical information.

The storage method introduces significant security risks. If a hacker gains physical access to your device or uses malware to read your local files, they can steal your session cookies.

With a stolen session cookie, an attacker can log into your accounts from a completely different computer without knowing your password.

To protect users and prevent cookie theft, developers use specific security flags when setting cookies:

The `HttpOnly` flag blocks JavaScript from reading the cookie file. This restriction prevents attackers from stealing your session tokens via Cross-Site Scripting attacks.

The `Secure` flag ensures the browser only transmits the cookie over encrypted HTTPS connections. This prevents bad actors from sniffing cookies on public Wi-Fi and in similar situations.

The `SameSite` flag restricts the browser from sending cookies during cross-site requests, which blocks Cross-Site Request Forgery attacks. It has two common values:

- `SameSite=Strict` prevents the browser from sending the cookie on any cross-site request.
- `SameSite=Lax` allows cookies on safe top-level navigation, such as clicking a link, but blocks them on cross-site form submissions and API requests.

Cookies also have massive privacy implications. First-party cookies only track your actions on the specific website you choose to visit. However, third-party cookies track you across entirely different websites.

Advertising networks place these cookies on thousands of popular sites. As you surf the net, the ad network reads the same third-party cookie repeatedly to build a detailed profile of your personal interests, search history, and online habits.

This invisible tracking creates a massive privacy concern because it allows corporations to monitor your digital life without your active knowledge.

Due to these threats, privacy laws like GDPR require websites to show cookie consent banners so you know what a website is doing with the cookies it is setting. These laws give you the legal right to reject tracking cookies.

In addition, modern browsers now block third-party tracking cookies by default to give users automated privacy protection.

cards.front:
What mitigation strategy effectively protects against credential stuffing attacks where stolen passwords are tested across multiple websites?

**A.** Storing passwords in plain text for faster verification.

**B.** Enforcing multi-factor authentication as a secondary verification step.

**C.** Requiring users to change their passwords every thirty days.

**D.** Blocking all login attempts from foreign IP addresses.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**B.** Enforcing multi-factor authentication as a secondary verification step.

## Lesson context

The digital world continues to face constant security threats, as attackers keep looking for weaknesses to steal data, disrupt systems, and extort money from unsuspecting users and platforms.

Let's look at some of these security threats and how to mitigate them.

**Phishing** is one of the most common security threats. In a phishing attack, criminals send fraudulent emails that mimic trusted corporations to trick users into clicking malicious links or sharing account passwords and other sensitive information.

To reduce phishing, companies must:

- Run regular security awareness training for users
- Employees must learn to spot suspicious sender addresses and urgent formatting
- Software teams must deploy email authentication protocols to block malicious messages before they reach the user inbox

**Malware** is another severe threat to users and developers. This category includes viruses, spyware, and ransomware.

Malicious actors use ransomware to encrypt a victim's computer files, and then they demand a large payment to unlock the data.

To prevent malware, software teams usually run automated updates and patch known software vulnerabilities. Security is a multi-layer thing, so users should also do their part by installing updates immediately and antimalware software on their devices.

**Credential stuffing attacks** target user authentication systems. Attackers use automated tools to test millions of stolen username and password combinations across different websites.

This kind of attack succeeds because many people reuse identical passwords across multiple platforms.

Companies can mitigate this threat by enforcing multi-factor authentication. Multi-factor authentication requires a second verification step, like a mobile authenticator app code, a one-time password (OTP), or email verification.

Even if a hacker steals the password, they cannot access the account without this secondary token.

**Distributed Denial of Service attacks** target system availability. Attackers flood a target website with massive amounts of fake internet traffic that suddenly overloads the server, crashes it, and blocks legitimate customers from accessing services.

To defend against these attacks, businesses use cloud-based traffic filtering services such as Cloudflare, Akamai, and AWS Shield.

These mitigation platforms analyze incoming traffic spikes. They filter out malicious data packets and allow normal user traffic to pass through.

Lastly, **insider threats** involve individuals within a company. This includes disgruntled employees who intentionally steal data or careless workers who accidentally leak information.

To counter this internal risk, companies enforce the principle of least privilege. This security standard ensures that workers only access the specific files necessary to complete their daily tasks.

Security teams also monitor system logs to flag unusual data downloads or unauthorized file access.

cards.front:
How do you completely disable a browser feature like geolocation for every user using the Permissions-Policy header?

**A.** Use `geolocation=(self)` in the policy header.

**B.** Use `geolocation=(*)` in the policy header.

**C.** Use `geolocation=()` with an empty list in the policy header.

**D.** Use `geolocation=(none)` in the policy header.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**C.** Use `geolocation=()` with an empty list in the policy header.

## Lesson context

CSP (Content Security Policy) and Permissions-Policy are two powerful HTTP security headers that help protect web applications by restricting what resources can load and what browser features a page can access.

Content Security Policy focuses primarily on resource loading. It acts as a safety filter for your frontend scripts, styles, and images.

Malicious actors often try to inject harmful scripts into vulnerable websites. A strong CSP stops these Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks by establishing a strict whitelist of trusted source domains.

When a server sends the CSP header, the browser reads the specific directives. For instance, the `script-src` directive tells the browser which domains can safely run JavaScript on the page.

If a hacker attempts to inject a malicious script from an unapproved external server, the browser detects the policy violation, drops the script instantly, and logs a security error.

CSP can also restrict image sources, form destinations, and stylesheet origins.

Permissions-Policy focuses on browser features and device hardware. It replaced the older Feature-Policy header.

This security mechanism allows site owners to explicitly enable or disable specific browser features for their own page and any embedded iframes, and prevents third-party snippets from abusing user privacy.

Using a Permissions-Policy header, you can control access to hardware like the webcam, microphone, and geolocation tracking.

For example, if your website does not need to know a user location, you can set the policy to block the geolocation API entirely. Even if an attacker compromises a script on your page, the browser will refuse to activate the tracking feature.

The implementation of Permissions-Policy uses a clear, structured header format that names the feature and defines its allowed origins.

To restrict a hardware feature strictly to your own domain, you use the `self` keyword enclosed in parentheses, such as `camera=(self)`. And if you want to disable a feature across the entire page for every user, you use an empty list instead, which looks like `geolocation=()`.

Combining both headers provides a solid defense for web applications. CSP locks down data delivery and prevents code injection, and Permissions-Policy guards the physical device and ensures privacy compliance.

Modern web developers use both tools to create a heavily fortified browsing environment.

---

cards.front:
What is the difference between direct and indirect identifiers when it comes to Personally Identifiable Information (PII)?

**A.** Direct identifiers are always encrypted, while indirect identifiers are always public.

**B.** Direct identifiers require user consent, while indirect identifiers do not.

**C.** Direct identifiers include IP addresses, while indirect identifiers include full names.

**D.** Direct identifiers pinpoint identity directly, while indirect identifiers do so indirectly.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**D.** Direct identifiers pinpoint identity directly, while indirect identifiers do so indirectly.

## Lesson context

User privacy is all about your right to control how your personal data is collected, used, and shared online. Modern privacy frameworks rely on several core building blocks to protect your digital footprint.

At the heart of privacy protection is **Personally Identifiable Information (PII).** PII is any data that can directly or indirectly pinpoint your identity.

Direct identifiers include your full name, home address, and national identification number, while indirect identifiers include your IP address, device serial number, or precise location history.

To keep this data safe, companies must maintain **Confidentiality**. Confidentiality ensures that your private data remains safe from unauthorized access through the use of strong encryption and access controls.

If an unauthorized third party reads your records or leaks your PII, your confidentiality has been broken.

Privacy frameworks enforce this through **Data Minimization** and **Purpose Limitation**. Data minimization states that companies should only collect the absolute minimum amount of PII required to complete a specific task.

Purpose limitation dictates that once a business collects your data for a specific reason, they cannot legally use it for anything else later on, such as selling your contact info to advertising networks.

These principles directly combat invasive digital tracking. **Tracking** is the continuous monitoring of your online movements across the internet.

Advertising networks use scripts, device fingerprinting, and browser history logs to trace your behavior and compile detailed profiles without your knowledge.

To protect against this tracking, user consent forms the bedrock of individual control. True privacy requires informed, explicit consent, meaning you must actively opt in to data tracking rather than being forced to do so.

Finally, **privacy laws guarantee the Right to be Forgotten,** also known as data erasure. This concept gives you the legal right to request that an organization permanently delete all your personal records and tracking history from its databases once you close your account.

You'll learn about those privacy laws and the bodies responsible for them in the next lecture.

---

cards.front:
What key benefit does using a `.env` file provide beyond security in different deployment environments?

**A.** It eliminates the need for any configuration files in production environments.

**B.** It requires separate codebases for development, testing, and production servers.

**C.** It automatically scales applications based on the environment variables set.

**D.** It allows the same codebase to behave differently by swapping the .env file per environment.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**D.** It allows the same codebase to behave differently by swapping the .env file per environment.

## Lesson context

The `.env` file and the `dotenv` library are tools used in modern software development to separate sensitive configuration data from application code.

A `.env` file is a plain text file placed at the root of a project directory that stores configuration settings and secrets as key-value pairs.

Instead of hardcoding API keys, database passwords, or port numbers directly into your source code and risking exposing them if the code is pushed to a public repository like GitHub, developers save them locally in this file.

The structure of a `.env` file is straightforward:

```bash
PORT=3000
DB_HOST=localhost
API_KEY=xyz123secretkey
```

Because this file contains highly sensitive keys, it is standard practice to add `.env` to the project `.gitignore` file so it is never tracked by Git.

The `dotenv` package is a lightweight module that connects the `.env` file to your application.

When your program starts, `dotenv` reads the `.env` file, parses the keys, and injects them into the runtime environment. In a Node.js application, for example, you initialize the package at the very top of your entry file. Once loaded, the variables become accessible globally through the `process.env` object.

```javascript
const express = require('express');
const app = express();

// initialize and configure dotenv
require('dotenv').config();

// access the variables securely from the environment
const port = process.env.PORT || 5000;
const apiKey = process.env.API_KEY;

app.get('/', (req, res) => {
  res.send(`Connected successfully using API Key: ${apiKey}`);
});

app.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`Server running on port ${port}`);
});
```

Using this setup offers two major benefits. First, it improves security by keeping private credentials out of source code. Second, it provides flexibility by allowing the same codebase to behave differently across development, testing, and production environments simply by swapping out the local `.env` file on each respective hosting server.

cards.front:
What is the purpose of setting up an automated DSAR (Data Subject Access Request) system for global privacy compliance?

**A.** To securely find, export, or permanently erase a user's entire data history upon request.

**B.** To prevent the unauthorized tracking of minors through age-verification gates.

**C.** To designate an internal expert to oversee privacy architecture.

**D.** To detect user geographic location and display appropriate cookie banners.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Answer

**A.** To securely find, export, or permanently erase a user's entire data history upon request.

## Lesson context

Regional privacy laws are legal structures enacted by specific countries or states to protect their citizens' personal data. Because the internet has no borders, you must follow these rules based entirely on where your users live, regardless of where your company is based.

**The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)** protects individuals inside the European Union and has been looked at by everyone as the model for global privacy rules. It demands that websites get strict, clear consent before tracking anyone, meaning you cannot use pre-ticked boxes or trick users into sharing data.

The GDPR also grants users massive rights over their data, including the right to view exactly what data a company holds on them and the right to demand its total deletion. Violating these rules carries immense financial penalties.

**The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA)**, along with its update, the CPRA, guards the data rights of consumers in California. Instead of forcing companies to use strict opt-in checkboxes like the EU, this law focuses heavily on giving users the right to opt out of data sharing.

CCPA specifically requires businesses to place a clear, easy-to-find link on their homepage that reads "Do Not Sell My Personal Information," allowing users to block third-party tracking instantly.

**The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA)** is a United States federal law designed to protect the privacy of children under the age of 13. It places strict restrictions on operators of websites and online services that are either directed at children or have actual knowledge that they are collecting data from them.

In addition, COPPA requires companies to post a clear privacy policy, provide direct notice to parents, and obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing any personal information from a child.

**The Data Protection Act (DPA)** is the principal data privacy framework enacted by the UK government to govern how personal data is processed. The DPA works alongside the UK GDPR, ensuring that personal data is handled lawfully, fairly, and transparently.

Under the DPA, individuals have robust rights, such as the right to access their information or request its deletion and strict data governance standards, which have been further updated to simplify compliance and mandate formal internal complaints processes for handling data grievances.

Apart from the laws already mentioned, other countries and regions around the world have their own strict data privacy frameworks to protect their residents' digital footprints. For example, **Nigeria has NDPA, the Nigeria Data Protection Act**, and **India has the DPDP Act, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act**.

To conform with these laws, you don't want to build unique websites for every territory separately. Instead, software teams manage compliance globally by following four core engineering and structural steps:

- **Build location-aware consent banners:** Your system detects the user's geographic location to dynamically display cookie banners that match their local privacy regulations.
- **Set up an automated DSAR system:** You must implement an automated backend workflow that securely finds, exports, or permanently erases a user's entire data history upon their legal request.
- **Practice strict data minimization and age-gating:** Your platform should only collect the absolute minimum data required to function while using age-verification gates to prevent the unauthorized tracking of minors.
- **Employ a data protection officer (DPO):** You need to designate an internal expert or external consultant to oversee your privacy architecture, manage legal risks, and act as the main point of contact for regulatory authorities.

## Key idea

A persistent tunnel is one that uses the same URL after exiting and restarting Visual Studio. Having a URL that doesn't change can be useful when integrating a web app with an external service. For example, implementing a GitHub webhook, or developing an API to integrate with a Power Platform app. In such cases, you might need to specify the callback URL to the external service. With a persistent tunnel, the external service URL only needs to be configured once. Using a temporary tunnel, the tunnel URL must be configured each time Visual Studio restarts.

*Persistent* doesn't mean the tunnel works when Visual Studio isn't open. A tunnel URL connects to the local machine only if the ASP.NET Core project that the tunnel URL connects to is running in Visual Studio.

A temporary tunnel is fine when the dev tunnel URL needs to work for a short time. For example, sharing in-progress work on a web app with others, or testing an app on an external device. In some cases, it might be best to get a new URL each time Visual Studio starts.

**Use .http files in Visual Studio 2022 — Azure Key Vault**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

[Azure Key Vault](https://github.com/azure/key-vault/general/overview) is one of several key management solutions in Azure that can be used for secrets management. Of the three secrets stores currently supported for `.http` files, Key Vault is the best choice for sharing secrets across different users. The other two options—[ASP.NET User Secrets](https://github.com/dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs/blob/c8ab8d7254e1b3cafa82eee538939c82d88cc8e5/aspnetcore/test/http-files.md#aspnet-core-user-secrets) and [DPAPI encryption](https://github.com/dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs/blob/c8ab8d7254e1b3cafa82eee538939c82d88cc8e5/aspnetcore/test/http-files.md#dpapi-encryption)—aren't easily shared.

To use a value from Azure Key Vault, you must be signed into Visual Studio with an account that has access to the desired Key Vault.
Define a variable in an environment file with the metadata to access the secret. The variable is named `AKVSecret` in the following example:

```json
{
  "dev": {
    "AKVSecret": {
      "provider": "AzureKeyVault",
      "secretName": "SecretInKeyVault",
      "resourceId": "/subscriptions/3a914c59-8175a9e0e540/resourceGroups/my-key-vault-rg/providers/Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/my-key-vault-01182024"
    }
  }
}
```

The variable `AKVSecret` pulls its value from Azure Key Vault. The following properties are defined on `AKVSecret`:

| Name         | Description                                             |
|--------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| provider     | For Key Vault, always use `AzureKeyVault`.              |
| secretName   | Name of the secret to extract.                          |
| resourceId   | Azure resource ID for the specific Key Vault to access. |

The value for the `resourceId` property can be found in the Azure portal. Go to **Settings > Properties** to find it. For `secretName`, use the name of the secret that appears on the **Secrets** page in the Azure portal.

For example, the following `.http` file has a request that uses this secret value.

```http
GET 
X-AKV-SECRET: 
```

## Key idea

The format for an HTTP request is `HTTPMethod URL HTTPVersion`, all on one line, where:

* `HTTPMethod` is the HTTP method to use, for example:
  * [OPTIONS](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods/OPTIONS)
  * [GET](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods/GET)
  * [HEAD](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods/HEAD)
  * [POST](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods/POST)
  * [PUT](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods/PUT)
  * [PATCH](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods/PATCH)
  * [DELETE](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods/DELETE)
  * [TRACE](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods/TRACE)
  * [CONNECT](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Methods/CONNECT)
* `URL` is the URL to send the request to. The URL can include query string parameters. The URL doesn't have to point to a local web project. It can point to any URL that Visual Studio can access.
* `HTTPVersion` is optional and specifies the HTTP version that should be used, that is, `HTTP/1.1`, `HTTP/2`, or `HTTP/3`.

A file can contain multiple requests by using lines with `###` as delimiters. The following example showing three requests in a file illustrates this syntax:

```http
GET https://localhost:7220/weatherforecast

###

GET https://localhost:7220/weatherforecast?date=2023-05-11&location=98006

###

GET https://localhost:7220/weatherforecast HTTP/3

###
```

cards.front:
**Integration tests in ASP.NET Core — Customize the `WebApplicationFactory` with test configurations**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

There are various ways to supply test-specific configurations to the running web application via `WebApplicationFactory`.

1. Using `ConfigureHostConfiguration`: override the `CreateHost` method and call `builder.ConfigureHostConfiguration` as follows:

    ```csharp
    private static readonly KeyValuePair<string, string?>[] s_inMemorySettings = new KeyValuePair<string, string?>[]
    {
        new("TestConfigKey", "TestConfigValue"),
    };

    protected override IHost CreateHost(IHostBuilder builder)
    {
        builder.ConfigureHostConfiguration(builder =>
        {
            builder.AddInMemoryCollection(s_inMemorySettings);
        });
        return base.CreateHost(builder);
    }
    ```

    Using this approach, the configuration source added via `ConfigureHostConfiguration` will be enumerated before the entry point is called, and the configurations will be passed to the entry point via `args`. The actual configuration source isn't preserved.

    > Make sure you pass `args` to `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` call. Otherwise, the configurations will not take effect.

2. Using `ConfigureAppConfiguration`: override the `ConfigureWebHost` method and call `builder.ConfigureAppConfiguration` as follows:

    ```csharp
    private static readonly KeyValuePair<string, string?>[] s_inMemorySettings = new KeyValuePair<string, string?>[]
    {
        new("TestConfigKey", "TestConfigValue"),
    };

    protected override void ConfigureWebHost(IWebHostBuilder builder)
    {
        base.ConfigureWebHost(builder);
        builder.ConfigureAppConfiguration(builder =>
        {
            builder.AddInMemoryCollection(s_inMemorySettings);
        });
    }
    ```

    Using this approach, the configuration source added via `ConfigureAppConfiguration` is preserved, but it's only available after the web application is built. If you try to access the configuration before `WebApplicationBuilder.Build` is called, the configurations will not be available.

3. Starting in .NET 11 Preview 7, you can override a new `ConfigureWebApplicationBuilder` method as follows:

    ```csharp
    private static readonly KeyValuePair<string, string?>[] s_inMemorySettings = new KeyValuePair<string, string?>[]
    {
        new("TestConfigKey", "TestConfigValue"),
    };

    protected override void ConfigureWebApplicationBuilder(IHostApplicationBuilder hostApplicationBuilder)
    {
        hostApplicationBuilder.Configuration.AddInMemoryCollection(s_inMemorySettings);
        base.ConfigureWebApplicationBuilder(hostApplicationBuilder);
    }
    ```

    Using this approach, the configuration source added via `ConfigureWebApplicationBuilder` is preserved, and is also available immediately after `WebApplication.CreateBuilder` returns.

---

**ASP.NET Core load/stress testing**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

Load testing and stress testing are important to ensure a web app is performant and scalable. Load and stress testing have different goals even though they often share similar tests.

**Load tests**: Test whether the app can handle a specified load of users for a certain scenario while still satisfying the response goal. The app is run under normal conditions.

**Stress tests**: Test app stability when running under extreme conditions, often for a long period of time. The tests place high user load, either spikes or gradually increasing load on the app, or they limit the app's computing resources.

Stress tests determine if an app under stress can recover from failure and gracefully return to expected behavior. Under stress, the app is run at abnormally high stress.

[Azure Load Testing](https://github.com/azure/load-testing/overview-what-is-azure-load-testing) is a fully managed load-testing service that enables you to generate high-scale load. The service simulates traffic for apps, regardless of where they're hosted. Azure Load Testing Preview enables you to use existing Apache JMeter scripts to generate high-scale load.

[Visual Studio 2019 load testing](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/devops/cloud-based-load-testing-service-eol/) has been deprecated. The corresponding Azure DevOps cloud-based load testing service has been closed.

## Key idea

```csharp
using Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Builder;

namespace Contoso.MyExtension;

public static class TestingPlatformBuilderHook
{
    public static void AddExtensions(ITestApplicationBuilder testApplicationBuilder, string[] arguments)
        => testApplicationBuilder.AddMyExtension();
}
```

The method must:

* Be `public static`.
* Have a first parameter of type `Microsoft.Testing.Platform.Builder.ITestApplicationBuilder`.
* Have a second parameter of type `string[]` (the command-line arguments passed to the test host). You can ignore it if your extension doesn't need it.

Each manifest entry identifies an assembly and a `TestingPlatformBuilderHook` type to invoke. MTP reports every loaded extension in terminal output and fails the run if a manifest, assembly, type, or hook is invalid. Set an entry's `enabled` property to `false` to disable it without deleting the manifest.

**Build extensions for Microsoft.Testing.Platform (MTP) — The `Include` GUID is a random identifier**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

The GUID in the `Include` attribute is **not** the same as your extension's [`IExtension.Uid`](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/core/testing/microsoft-testing-platform-architecture.md#the-iextension-interface). It's a registration identifier used by the MSBuild task to deduplicate hooks across NuGet references and (in a few well-known cases) to order them.

When you author a new extension, generate a brand new GUID and hard-code it in your props file. Some ways to generate one:

* PowerShell: `[guid]::NewGuid()`
* Visual Studio: **Tools** > **Create GUID**
* `uuidgen` on Linux and macOS

> Never copy a GUID from another extension's props file (whether shipped by Microsoft or by a third party). Two extensions that share the same `Include` value are treated as duplicates: only one hook is invoked, so your extension silently fails to register.

> Once you ship a GUID, treat it as permanent. Changing it in a later release is harmless on its own, but reusing the *old* value for a different hook in a future package version can confuse consumers who have both versions in their dependency graph during an upgrade.

## Key idea

The `CreateTestSessionAsync` method is called at the start of the test session and is used to initialize the test framework. The API accepts a `CreateTestSessionContext` object and returns a `CreateTestSessionResult`.

```csharp
public sealed class CreateTestSessionContext : TestSessionContext

}
```

The return object is a `CreateTestSessionResult`:

```csharp

{
    public string? WarningMessage { get; set; }
    public string? ErrorMessage { get; set; }
    public bool IsSuccess { get; set; }
}
```

cards.front:
**Microsoft.Testing.Platform (MTP) config options — CLI options in testconfig.json**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

Before MTP 2.3.0, extension features such as [crash dump](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/core/testing/microsoft-testing-platform-crash-hang-dumps.md), [hang dump](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/core/testing/microsoft-testing-platform-crash-hang-dumps.md), [retry](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/core/testing/microsoft-testing-platform-retry.md), [TRX reports](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/core/testing/microsoft-testing-platform-test-reports.md), and [code coverage](https://github.com/dotnet/docs/blob/6b94bd8af573d315cd45b8d7dd8adc38bb3f6693/docs/core/testing/microsoft-testing-platform-code-coverage.md) aren't configurable via *testconfig.json*. These features are configured exclusively through command-line arguments.

Starting with MTP 2.3.0, MTP can read CLI options from *testconfig.json* through `IConfiguration`. This support includes extension options, so you can use JSON entries for options that you don't want to pass on the command line each run. Command-line arguments still take precedence.

Configuration doesn't install or register an extension. Each test application must reference the package that provides an extension option, either directly or through a test SDK configuration or profile. Otherwise, the option remains unrecognized whether you put it in *testconfig.json* or on the command line.

Use the `commandLineOptions` object for active options. Omit the leading `--` from each key. Use `true` for a zero-argument option, and use `false` to disable an option. For one argument, use a string or number. For repeated or multiple arguments, use an array:

```json
{ "commandLineOptions": {
  "report-trx": true,
  "report-trx-filename": "results.trx",
  "filter-uid": ["test-1", "test-2"]
} }
```

MTP treats a string or number scalar as the first argument of an argument-bearing option. To pass a Boolean argument, use an array such as `[true]` or `[false]`. The array distinguishes the argument from a Boolean presence value.

MTP validates configured entries like command-line entries. Unknown options, invalid values, and values with the wrong arity fail validation. An explicit command-line option overrides the corresponding `commandLineOptions` entry.

Bootstrap-only options run before MTP loads configuration. Don't put `config-file`, `diagnostic`, `diagnostic-output-directory`, `diagnostic-file-prefix`, `diagnostic-verbosity`, `diagnostic-synchronous-write`, or `enable-dynamic-extensions` in `commandLineOptions`.

---

cards.front:
**Microsoft.Testing.Platform overview - .NET test runner — MTP pillars**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

This new testing platform is built on the .NET Developer Experience Testing team's experience and aims to address the challenges encountered since the release of .NET Core in 2016. While there's a high level of compatibility between the .NET Framework and the .NET Core/.NET, some key features like the plugin-system and the new possible form factors of .NET compilations have made it complex to evolve or fully support the new runtime feature with the current [VSTest platform](https://github.com/microsoft/vstest) architecture.

The main driving factors for the evolution of the new testing platform are detailed in the following:

* **Determinism**: Ensuring that running the same tests in different contexts (local, CI) will produce the same result. The new runtime does not rely on reflection or any other dynamic .NET runtime feature to coordinate a test run.

* **Runtime transparency**: The test runtime does not interfere with the test framework code, it does not create isolated contexts like `AppDomain` or `AssemblyLoadContext`, and it does not use reflection or custom assembly resolvers.

* **Compile-time registration of extensions**: Extensions, such as test frameworks and in/out-of-process extensions, are registered during compile-time to ensure determinism and to facilitate detection of inconsistencies.

* **Zero dependencies**: The core of the platform is a single .NET assembly, `Microsoft.Testing.Platform.dll`, which has no dependencies other than the supported runtimes.

* **Hostable**: The test runtime can be hosted in any .NET application. While a console application is commonly used to run tests, you can create a test application in any type of .NET application. This allows you to run tests within special contexts, such as devices or browsers, where there may be limitations.

* **Support all .NET form factors**: Support current and future .NET form factors, including Native AOT.

* **Performant**: Finding the right balance between features and extension points to avoid bloating the runtime with non-fundamental code. The new test platform is designed to "orchestrate" a test run, rather than providing implementation details on how to do it.

* **Extensible enough**: The new platform is built on extensibility points to allow for maximum customization of runtime execution. It allows you to configure the test process host, observe the test process, and consume information from the test framework within the test host process.

* **Single module deploy**: The hostability feature enables a single module deploy model, where a single compilation result can be used to support all extensibility points, both out-of-process and in-process, without the need to ship different executable modules.

---

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.

## Key idea

The telemetry feature doesn't collect personal data, such as usernames or email addresses. It doesn't scan your code and doesn't extract project-level data, such as repository, or author, it extracts the name of your executable and sends it in hashed form.

It doesn't extract the contents of any data files accessed or created by your apps, dumps of any memory occupied by your apps' objects, or the contents of the clipboard.

The data is sent securely to Microsoft servers using Azure Monitor technology, held under restricted access, and published under strict security controls from secure Azure Storage systems.

Protecting your privacy is important to Microsoft! If you suspect the telemetry is collecting sensitive data or the data is being insecurely or inappropriately handled, file an issue in the [microsoft/testfx](https://github.com/microsoft/testfx) GitHub repository or send an email to [dotnet@microsoft.com](mailto:dotnet@microsoft.com) for investigation.

cards.front:
**Migration guide from VSTest to Microsoft.Testing.Platform (MTP) — Console.InputEncoding preservation**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

If you run your tests in a console where the codepage was explicitly changed (for example, in Azure DevOps, the codepage is set to 65001 which corresponds to UTF8), the behavior can be different between VSTest and MTP.

- With MTP, that encoding is always preserved.
- With VSTest not running in isolation mode (the default behavior of vstest.console), that encoding is preserved, similar to MTP.
- With VSTest running in isolation mode (the default behavior of `dotnet test`), that encoding isn't preserved in the testhost, which is the process that runs the tests.

> The reason the encoding isn't preserved with VSTest isolation mode is that the testhost process is started with `CreateNoWindow = true`. So it's not attached to the original console.

If you have a test that starts yet another child process and redirects its standard output, you might face issues if all the following apply:

- The console codepage is set to 65001 (UTF8). This can be the case on CI but generally not locally. To get a local behavior similar to in CI, run `chcp 65001` before running the tests.
- The child process is started with non-UTF8 encoding. This can also happen if your own test also sets `CreateNoWindow = true`.

This is especially problematic when the child process doesn't expect to see the UTF8 BOM (Byte-Order-Mark) byte, which it might get in the previous scenario on .NET Framework.

As this behavior difference is likely to be problematic specifically for the BOM byte, a workaround is to set InputEncoding during assembly initialization to UTF8 without BOM:

```csharp
Console.InputEncoding = new UTF8Encoding(encoderShouldEmitUTF8Identifier: false);
```

A different workaround for that is to not use `CreateNoWindow = true` for child processes that redirect standard input.

cards.front:
**Migration guide from VSTest to Microsoft.Testing.Platform (MTP) — Update `dotnet test` invocations**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

Command line options of `dotnet test` are divided into two categories: build-related arguments and test-related ones.

The build-related arguments are irrelevant to the test platform and as such don't need to be updated for the new platform. Build-related arguments are listed here:

- `-a|--arch <ARCHITECTURE>`
- `--artifacts-path <ARTIFACTS_DIR>`
- `-c|--configuration <CONFIGURATION>`
- `-f|--framework <FRAMEWORK>`
- `-e|--environment <NAME="VALUE">`
- `--interactive`
- `--no-build`
- `--nologo`
- `--no-restore`
- `-o|--output <OUTPUT_DIRECTORY>`
- `--os <OS>`
- `-r|--runtime <RUNTIME_IDENTIFIER>`
- `-v|--verbosity <LEVEL>`

Although `--arch` remains a build-related option, it replaces the architecture that VSTest selects through `RunConfiguration.TargetPlatform`. Pass `--arch` to `dotnet test` itself, before any `--` separator.

For example, migrate this VSTest project command:

```dotnetcli
dotnet test MyTests.csproj -c Debug -- RunConfiguration.TargetPlatform=x86 /Parallel
```

For .NET 10 SDK and later versions, use this MTP command:

```dotnetcli
dotnet test --project MyTests.csproj -c Debug --arch x86
```

Replace `x86` with `x64` to target x64. MTP runs test modules in parallel by default, so `/Parallel` doesn't need a replacement. To limit module-level parallelism, use `--max-parallel-test-modules <NUMBER>`.

> You can't combine `--solution` with `--arch`, `--os`, or `--runtime`. These options set `RuntimeIdentifier` as a global MSBuild property, and solution builds don't support a global `RuntimeIdentifier`. To test a solution across architectures, invoke each test project separately or set `RuntimeIdentifier` in the individual test projects.

For example, replace these four solution-level VSTest commands:

```dotnetcli
dotnet test MySolution.sln -c Debug -- RunConfiguration.TargetPlatform=x86 /Parallel
dotnet test MySolution.sln -c Release -- RunConfiguration.TargetPlatform=x86 /Parallel
dotnet test MySolution.sln -c Debug -- RunConfiguration.TargetPlatform=x64 /Parallel
dotnet test MySolution.sln -c Release -- RunConfiguration.TargetPlatform=x64 /Parallel
```

For .NET 10 SDK and later versions, use a project-level matrix:

```powershell
$testProjects = @("tests/A.Tests/A.Tests.csproj", "tests/B.Tests/B.Tests.csproj")
$testRunFailed = $false
foreach ($configuration in "Debug", "Release") {
    foreach ($architecture in "x86", "x64") {
        foreach ($testProject in $testProjects) {
            dotnet test --project $testProject -c $configuration --arch $architecture
            if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) {
                $testRunFailed = $true
            }
        }
    }
}
if ($testRunFailed) {
    throw "One or more test runs failed."
}
```

**MSTEST0025: Use 'Assert.Fail' instead of an always-failing assert — Rule description**

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Key idea

Using `Assert.Fail` over an always-failing assertion call provides clearer intent and better documentation for the code.

When you encounter an assertion that always fails (for example, `Assert.IsTrue(false)`), it might not be immediately obvious to someone reading the code why the assertion is there or what condition it's trying to check. This can lead to confusion and wasted time for developers who come across the code later on.

In contrast, using `Assert.Fail` allows you to provide a custom failure message, making it clear why the assertion is failing and what specific condition or scenario it's addressing. This message serves as documentation for the intent behind the assertion, helping other developers understand the purpose of the assertion without needing to dive deep into the code.

Overall, using `Assert.Fail` promotes clarity, documentation, and maintainability in your codebase, making it a better choice over an always failing assertion call.

Explain the key behavior described by this topic.
